\chapter*{Abstract}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Abstract}

This work is the first volume of \emph{Void and Form}, proposed as a theory of formulability: an account of the conditions under which mathematical, logical, and physical description can become stable enough to be stated. It does not ask what emerges from a presupposed ``nothing''. It asks under which conditions formal description is possible at all. The starting point is the minimal condition of every formal theory: distinguishable positions. Without such distinguishability, no relation, judgement, equation, map, representation, truth-value, or falsehood can be formulated. \emph{Void} names this pre-formal boundary. It is not the empty set, not the empty type, and not a physical nothing; it is the absence of the domain in which those notions could already occur.

Once distinguishability is granted, the boundary receives a formal representative: two non-collapsing occurrences that exhaust their carrier. The claim that this is the minimal entry is a boundary argument, not itself an Agda theorem; the theorem begins only after the representative has been supplied. Inside intensional Martin-L\"of type theory, checked by Agda under \AgdaFlag{safe} and \AgdaFlag{without-K}, the record \texttt{Distinction} represents the threshold as a carrier, two separated boundary points, and an exhaustive cover. Every such structure has the canonical normal form \texttt{Two}; its endomorphisms exhaust to four cases; representing those cases with separation, complete realisation, and no surplus forces a four-element structure with complete simple adjacency; and the resulting structure points back to the distinction from which it arose.

The argument is therefore not a derivation from an ontological beginning. It is an analysis of the conditions under which formal theories can be formulated, followed by the machine-checked derivation of the first non-trivial structure that necessarily appears once those conditions are represented. The formulability claim is the architectural reading of this whole dependency: the pre-formal boundary explains why the datum matters, the Agda development checks what the datum forces, and the later volume \emph{Form} tests how far the resulting invariant ledger can be read as a structure of physical description. The later arithmetic, spectral, and interpretive layers of the book unfold over that survivor. They do not supply a new generator.

\section*{Structural Schema}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Structural Schema}

\begin{description}
\item[Level 0: Void.] No type, no term, no carrier. The schematic marker is $\mathcal{V} \notin \mathit{Set}_\omega$. Void is not a stable endpoint in the sense of a foundation, because every act of positing already presupposes structure. It is therefore not refutably unstable; it is conceptually non-closable. This level is marked, not proved.

\item[Level 1: Information.] Information is understood in Bateson's minimal sense: a difference that makes a difference. Without distinction, an occurrence carries no information; a single undifferentiated occurrence collapses back into the boundary. Information therefore presupposes distinction. The binary shape is the first non-collapsing candidate in the boundary argument, because every further difference already relies on one position being told from another.

\item[Level 2: Two.] The formal representative used here is \texttt{data Two : Set where L R : Two}. It contains two separated points and no third generator. It is not a truth-value object; it is the normal form of distinction once the binary data have been granted. From this level onward the formal threshold is crossed: MLTT and Agda can execute the consequences of the datum they have received.

\item[Level 3: Logic.] Formal systems operate on structures in which distinguishable positions are already available. Relation, morphism, judgement, and equation do not construct that availability; they use it. MLTT is the clean carrier used here, not the origin of the cut.

\item[Level 4: Mathematics.] The machine-checked chain is the mathematical core: every \texttt{Distinction} is isomorphic to \texttt{Two}; the endomorphisms of \texttt{Two} have exactly four cases; representing those cases under separation, complete realisation, and no surplus forces the four-element closure, unique up to isomorphism; and the closure returns the originating distinction. No further generator is introduced.

\item[Level 5: Form.] The interpretive volume reads the stability conditions of distinction structurally. Two distinguishable occurrences collapse if neither origin nor position can distinguish them. Non-identity of origin gives the germ of temporal order; non-coincidence gives the germ of spatial separation. Space and time are not asserted as primitive entities here. They name conditions under which distinction does not collapse.

\item[Level 6: Physics.] Physics enters as interpretation of the preceding structural conditions by an observer who already operates inside them. Form is not physics; it is the structure from which physical description can be read.

\item[Level 7: Contingency.] Necessity stops before complete worldly specification. The preceding levels fix conditions, not the full concrete world that satisfies them.

\item[Level 8: Induction.] No new external generator is postulated. More complex structures are read as repeated applications and stabilisations of the original distinction. Induction is the law of that repetition. This is a structural reading, not a reductionist claim about all mathematics.
\end{description}

The first two levels are not formal statements inside a type system. They state the conditions under which formal statements can appear. They are not left informal because notation is missing, but because they concern the possibility of introducing notation in the first place. The passage from boundary to \texttt{Distinction} is therefore the first formal grant, not a theorem about the boundary itself. From Level 2 onward the formal theory begins, and the claims are expressible and checkable inside it.

The proposed theory of formulability is not an additional ninth level. It is the reading of the chain as a whole. If Level 0 and Level 1 are removed, the formal code loses its reason for beginning with distinction. If Level 2 through Level 4 fail, the claim loses its checked kernel. If Level 5 through Level 8 are treated as theorems rather than structural readings, the claim overreaches. The work is held together only because these statuses are kept separate and ordered.

\section*{Inheritance}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Inheritance}

None of the ideas in this work are ownerless. The derivation is a single thread; what follows names the hands that spun it.

The starting point---that a distinction, not a thing, is the irreducible atom of form---belongs to George Spencer-Brown. This work does not begin with a distinguishing operation, but with the minimal structure in which a distinction is already realised. The question is not how a distinction is drawn, but what must be given for a distinction to be stably present.

That the second layer can be made rigorous at all is owed to the constructivists. Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer insisted that existence demands a witness. Arend Heyting gave that demand algebraic form. Haskell Curry and William Alvin Howard revealed that proofs and programs are the same act. Per Martin-L\"of forged these insights into a type theory strong enough to carry mathematics, and Vladimir Voevodsky showed what must be given up---axiom K, uniqueness of identity proofs---if homotopy is to be taken seriously. This work does not make type theory the origin of the cut; it uses type theory as the disciplined threshold at which the consequences of the cut can be executed without smuggling in additional structure.

The combinatorial backbone has older roots. Leonhard Euler first counted vertices, edges, and faces as a single invariant. Arthur Cayley classified graphs by their symmetries. Garrett Birkhoff established when a representation is canonical. Under the stated constraints, the four-element closure is forced and unique up to isomorphism.

That spectral properties of this structure are determined rather than chosen follows the tradition of Joseph Fourier, Pierre-Simon Laplace, and David Hilbert. The Laplacian spectrum of the resulting structure is inherited, not imposed.

What determines invariance is the automorphism group. Evariste Galois showed that solvability is a property of the group, not the equation. Here, the automorphism group of the closure structure plays that role: only quantities invariant under it factor through the canonical base.

The categorical perspective---that structure is characterized by the maps it admits---descends from William Lawvere and the semantic tradition of Alfred Tarski.

What is new here is not the question but the execution. The constraints are explicit, minimal, and mechanically checked once the formal threshold is crossed. The claim that this amounts to a theory of formulability is therefore not a decorative title placed above the proof; it is the architectural consequence of making the dependency from boundary, to distinction, to closure, to invariant ledger explicit.

\mainmatter

\part*{The Ontological Threshold}
\addcontentsline{toc}{part}{The Ontological Threshold}

\chapter{What Void Does Not Name}
\label{ch:void-does-not-name}

\section{The Name Does Not Create An Object}
\label{sec:void:name-not-object}

The word \emph{Void} is easily misunderstood because ordinary language turns every name into a thing. If the word names something, one is tempted to ask what kind of thing it names: an empty region, an empty set, an empty type, a first object, a background container. Each of those readings arrives too late. A set is already a form of collection. A type is already a domain of possible inhabitants. A region is already separated from another region. A container already distinguishes inside from outside.

Void names the condition before those distinctions have obtained. It is not an object hidden behind objects. It is the absence of the field in which objecthood could already be stated. It is not silence inside a language. It is the boundary before the first difference that would let a language say anything at all.

This is why the first movement of the book cannot be an Agda theorem. Agda works with terms, types, judgements, constructors, and equality. Each of these already belongs to a field of distinguishable positions. To ask Agda to prove the necessity of that field would be to ask the instrument to generate the condition under which instruments exist. The theorem begins later. The boundary comes first.

The danger at the beginning is therefore twofold. If Void is treated as a mathematical object, the argument has smuggled in the very form whose origin is being investigated. If Void is treated as a poetic nothing, the argument loses contact with proof. The path between these failures is narrow: Void is a boundary name. It marks the absence of relation, comparison, representation, judgement, and equation; it does not pretend to be a formal inhabitant of the calculus that later begins.

\section{The Boundary Before Reading}
\label{sec:void:boundary-before-reading}

The boundary is not a hidden substance behind the world. It is the point at which the question ``what is there?'' has not yet earned the grammar in which it could be asked. A question separates itself from its answer. A name separates itself from what it names. A proof separates premise, transformation, and conclusion. Even denial separates what is denied from the denial that attempts to erase it.

Void is therefore not the first item in an inventory. It is what remains when inventory has not yet begun. The first form that can survive contact with representation is not an object but a cut: a minimal separation by which a mark can differ from what is unmarked, a side can differ from another side, and a judgement can have a place to stand.

This is the first discipline of the book. The opening language must not pretend that the cut is already a theorem inside a calculus. The calculus arrives later. The boundary is the pressure that makes arrival possible.

\chapter{Why Formal Systems Cannot Begin Themselves}
\label{ch:formal-systems-cannot-begin-themselves}

\section{The First Judgement Already Separates}
\label{sec:formal-systems:first-judgement}

A formal system does not wake up in a blank world. It begins with marks that can be repeated, variables that can be substituted, terms that can be judged, equations whose sides can be compared, and rules whose premises can be separated from their conclusions. Even the most austere calculus already distinguishes a judgement from its object, a term from its type, a premise from the inference it licenses.

That is not a defect in formal systems. It is what makes formalisation possible. But it means that no formal system can be the absolute origin of distinction. The first formal line already uses the separation it might wish to analyse. A judgement of the form $a : A$ has two positions. An equality $x \equiv y$ has two sides. A function $A \to B$ has source and target. A context has entries that can be addressed one after another. The machinery of proof begins only after some difference can be held stable enough to be used.

This book therefore refuses the wrong order. Martin-L\"of type theory is not presented as the metaphysical ground from which distinction is manufactured. It is the formal language used here after the ontological threshold has been reached. Once the cut is represented inside that language, the type checker can judge the consequences. Before that point, the question is not yet internal to type theory. It concerns what any type theory, any logic, any calculus, and any act of representation must already presuppose.

\section{The Status Of The Opening Claim}
\label{sec:introduction:claim-status}

The opening claim is deliberately modest in its formal status and severe in its consequence. It does not say that an event occurred in time. It does not say that a physical particle appeared. It does not say that Agda proves an origin event. It says that representation is impossible without a cut.

The claim can be tested by trying to remove the cut. Remove the distinction between sign and signed, and no representation remains. Remove the distinction between two sides of an equation, and equality has nothing to compare. Remove the distinction between source and target, and no map remains. Remove the distinction between premise and conclusion, and no inference remains. What disappears in each case is not a technical convenience but the possibility of the form itself.

For that reason the reader is asked to keep five statuses separate throughout the book.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Boundary arguments} name what formalisation already presupposes. They are not Agda theorems.
\item \textbf{Formal representations} translate the boundary into explicit data that a selected proof assistant can manipulate.
\item \textbf{Machine-checked theorems} prove what follows from those data under the displayed rules.
\item \textbf{The formulability claim} is the architectural thesis that the checked chain exposes the first stable skeleton of formulability itself.
\item \textbf{Interpretive readings} belong to the companion volume \emph{Form}, where physical vocabulary is attached only after the formal record has closed.
\end{enumerate}

Confusing these statuses destroys the project. Treat the boundary argument as a theorem, and the beginning overclaims. Treat the checked theorems as metaphor, and the execution is lost. Treat the formulability claim as a slogan, and the chain loses its reason for being. Treat the physical readings as premises, and the numerology objection becomes justified. The book survives only if the statuses remain visible.

\chapter{Representation Requires A Cut}
\label{ch:representation-requires-cut}

\section{Presence Is Not Representation}
\label{sec:representation:not-presence}

Presence alone does not represent. A single undifferentiated occurrence, with no position from which it can be read and no position to which it can be related, carries no representation. Representation begins only when something can appear \emph{as} something: a mark as a sign, a term as an inhabitant, a side as equal to another side, a map as connecting source to target.

This ``as'' is already a cut. It separates what is presented from the presentation through which it is available. Even the attempt to collapse them requires a relation of collapse, and that relation again has sides. The collapse cannot be stated without the distinction it denies.

The first cut is therefore not a decoration placed on an otherwise complete field. It is the condition under which a field can be read at all. Without it there is no error, because there is no proposition to fail. There is no identity, because there are no positions to identify. There is no object, because objecthood requires a boundary by which something is this and not everything indifferently.

\section{Sign, Object, And Reading}
\label{sec:representation:sign-object-reading}

Every representation contains a minimum drama: something stands, something is stood for, and some relation lets the standing count as such. Collapsing any side of that drama destroys representation rather than purifying it. If the sign is nothing but the signed, there is no sign. If the signed is nothing but the sign, there is no excess for the sign to carry. If the relation vanishes, the standing-as vanishes with it.

The cut is therefore not an optional philosophical gloss placed beside a theory of signs. It is the condition under which signs, terms, equations, maps, and measurements can be read at all. Representation does not begin with a populated world and then add difference as an annotation. Difference is the pressure that lets a world become readable as populated.

\chapter{Why The First Cut Is Binary}
\label{ch:first-cut-binary}

\section{Why One Is Not Enough}
\label{sec:representation:one-not-enough}

The temptation is to begin with one. One seems simpler than two, and an ontology that begins from one appears more austere than an ontology that begins from distinction. But one already hides the problem. To say ``one'' is to count, and counting requires the stability of a unit against what is not that unit. To name one is to distinguish the named from the act of naming. To point to one is to distinguish pointer, pointed, and the direction between them.

An absolutely undifferentiated one cannot carry a relation. It cannot be self-related, because self-relation distinguishes the relatum from the relation. It cannot be represented, because representation distinguishes representation from what is represented. It cannot even be asserted without a judgement in which the assertion and its content stand apart.

Thus one is not primitive enough. It is either too little, because it contains no relation and therefore no representation, or too much, because the moment it is named it has already borrowed the cut it was supposed to precede. The first stable form is not a solitary point. It is the minimal separation by which point, name, judgement, and relation become possible.

\section{Why Three Is Too Much At The Origin}
\label{sec:representation:three-too-much}

If one cannot carry representation, the next failure is to begin with more than the cut requires. Three positions already contain surplus. They allow a choice of middle, an order, a comparison of alternatives, or a residual place not explained by the first separation. None of that is forced by the mere condition that representation be possible.

The first cut requires two sides: this and not-this, mark and unmarked, left and right, source and target, term and type, side and side. A third place may appear later, but it cannot be smuggled into the origin without adding structure. It is an extra degree of freedom. The eliminative method will not tolerate it at the threshold.

This is the first shape of the later formal result. In MLTT, a carrier that presents exactly a covered binary distinction will be shown isomorphic to \texttt{Two}. That theorem is not the pre-formal argument itself. It is the checked echo of the same pressure after the boundary has been translated into formal data.

\section{The Minimal Survivor}
\label{sec:first-cut:minimal-survivor}

The binary cut is not selected because two is aesthetically pleasing. It survives because the alternatives fail at opposite ends. One does not yet give representation a relation. Three already gives representation more positions than the first necessity demands. Two is the narrow middle: enough for opposition, not enough for surplus.

This does not yet prove the Agda theorem \texttt{two-normal-form}. It prepares the ground on which that theorem will become legible. The theorem will say, inside the selected formal system, that any covered separated binary carrier is boundary-preservingly isomorphic to \texttt{Two}. The ontological threshold says something prior and weaker in form but stronger in reach: if representation is to begin at all, the first stable field cannot be unary and cannot require a third generator.

\chapter{Origin, Contact, And Non-Collapse}
\label{ch:origin-contact-non-collapse}

\section{Retrieval Requires Non-Collapse}
\label{sec:origin-contact:retrieval}

Two occurrences cannot be two if they share both the same origin and the same contact without remainder. If there is no difference of origin, no difference of contact, and no difference of position by which one can be recovered rather than the other, then there are not two occurrences. There is only collapse.

This point must be stated carefully. The argument does not yet introduce metric space, physical time, distance, duration, or motion. It says only that distinguishability forbids total coincidence. If two informational positions are retrievable as two, then some non-coincidence is already in force. If every condition of retrieval collapses, the two disappear.

\section{No Physics Yet}
\label{sec:origin-contact:no-physics-yet}

At the boundary, this is the germ of the later readings of time and space, but it is not yet physics. It is weaker and more primitive: two positions cannot be the same position in every respect relevant to their retrieval. Formal theories operate inside this field of retrievable difference. The field is not manufactured by the theory; it is what lets the theory have more than one place to write on.

\[
\begin{array}{c}
\text{representation possible} \\
\Downarrow \\
\text{two retrievable informational positions} \\
\Downarrow \\
\neg\bigl(\mathsf{SameOrigin} \wedge \mathsf{SameContact} \wedge \mathsf{NoSeparation}\bigr)
\end{array}
\]

The display is schematic meta-notation. It is not Agda code, and its arrows are not internal implication terms. It records the boundary that later receives a formal representative.

\chapter{The Information Field Before Theory}
\label{ch:information-field-before-theory}

\section{Position Before Measurement}
\label{sec:information-field:position-before-measurement}

Measurement begins later than distinguishability. To measure something, a procedure must already be able to return a value rather than another value, compare a mark with a scale, and keep the measured position apart from the act of measuring it. Before any unit can be introduced, the field must already admit retrievable positions.

This field is informational only in the primitive sense: something can be recovered as this rather than that. It is not a database, not a medium, not a physical substrate, and not an observer's mental state. It is the minimum readability without which no database, medium, substrate, observer, or equation can be specified.

\section{Theory Enters An Already Cut Field}
\label{sec:information-field:theory-enters}

Every formal theory enters through the same gate. It may choose different primitives, different equality principles, different universes, different tactics, or different computational kernels; but if it can state anything at all, it must distinguish statement from non-statement, rule from application, term from context, and success from failure.

The information field is therefore not a rival formalism. It is the pre-formal condition shared by formalisms that can read their own marks. Once a particular carrier is selected, the differences between proof assistants matter intensely. Before selection, the shared condition is simpler and harsher: there must be a cut.

\chapter{Formalisations Are Plural}
\label{ch:formalisations-are-plural}

\section{No Formal System Generates The Cut}
\label{sec:formalisations:no-system-generates-cut}

The boundary forces the need for a carrier; it does not force the concrete name of the carrier. Agda does not create the cut. MLTT does not create the cut. Coq, Lean, cubical systems, set-theoretic foundations, and other disciplined calculi would not create it either. At most, a formal system can receive the boundary as explicit data and then expose which consequences survive inside its rules.

This distinction matters because otherwise the book would confuse two necessities. The cut is necessary for representation. Agda is the chosen execution environment in which the consequences of one formal representative are checked. The first claim reaches beyond this implementation. The mechanised theorems do not.

\section{What A Carrier Must Discipline}
\label{sec:formalisations:carrier-discipline}

A proof assistant can carry this development only if it can keep the relevant pressures visible. It must let the formal representative state a carrier, two boundary positions, a separation witness, and a coverage principle. It must make case analysis explicit enough that hidden residues cannot pass as absence. It must distinguish construction from postulate, and it must let failed alternatives collapse by contradiction rather than by rhetoric.

For the present development, the carrier must also discipline equality, totality, and exhaustivity. Equality cannot be allowed to identify too much too soon. Functions cannot be partial procedures masquerading as proofs. Coverage cannot be inferred from the fact that only two names were written down. The formal language has to keep every one of these gates locked while the eliminative chain runs.

\section{MLTT As One Disciplined Carrier}
\label{sec:formalisations:mltt-one-carrier}

Intensional Martin-L\"of type theory provides such a carrier for this book. It makes constructions explicit, treats propositions as types, and forces proofs to appear as terms. Agda then exposes that discipline through a concrete checker. Under \AgdaFlag{safe}, no postulate can be smuggled into the file. Under \AgdaFlag{without-K}, equality is not flattened by uniqueness of identity proofs.

This is why MLTT and Agda enter here: not as metaphysical origin, and not as the only conceivable formal clothing of the argument, but as the expression in which the present execution is carried out. The proof that another assistant can carry the same structure would be a further theorem of translation or reconstruction. It is not assumed here, and it is not needed in order for the present file to run.

The formulability claim does not depend on Agda being metaphysically privileged. It depends on the fact that this execution is explicit enough to expose the dependency chain. Another carrier could strengthen the claim by reconstructing the same chain under different rules; it could also reveal exactly where the present chain depends on MLTT. Either outcome would be mathematical progress. What cannot be done is to dismiss the claim as mere style while ignoring the checked segment that gives it weight.

\section{What Remains Open}
\label{sec:formalisations:what-remains-open}

It remains open, in this volume, whether other proof assistants can carry Void with the same fidelity. The question is meaningful and sharp. A successful reconstruction would have to reproduce the boundary representative, the binary normal form, the endomorphism classification, the failure of three vertices, the closure at $K_4$, and the return from the invariant record to distinction without importing stronger principles that change the result.

Until such reconstructions are written, the honest statement is exact: this book mechanises Void in MLTT as implemented by Agda. It shows what follows there. It does not claim that Agda is the only possible witness, and it does not weaken the cut by admitting that plural formal carriers may exist. The cut is prior to the carrier. The carrier is where the consequences are executed.

\chapter{The Formal Threshold}
\label{ch:formal-threshold}

\section{The Tool: Agda as Executioner}
\label{sec:introduction:agda-as-executioner}

The machine enters only after the threshold has been crossed. Agda can verify that a term has the type it claims to have. It can verify that a case split is exhaustive, that a contradiction has no branch, that a construction uses no postulate, and that an alleged equality reduces to \texttt{refl}. It cannot verify, from nowhere, the pre-formal necessity of representation itself. That necessity is what makes formal verification possible in the first place.

This division is not a retreat. It is the contract that keeps the work honest. Before the threshold, the book argues that formalisation presupposes distinguishable positions. After the threshold, every claimed consequence is submitted to the type checker. The pre-formal argument does not pretend to be code. The formal development does not pretend to have generated its own condition of possibility.

This is also where the theory of formulability becomes testable rather than merely visionary. The vision says that formulability begins with distinction. The method receives that distinction as explicit data. The checker then decides whether the claimed normal form, classification, closure, and return to the datum actually follow. If the chain breaks, the formulability claim breaks with it. If the chain holds, the claim is no longer only philosophical language; it has a formal spine.

The compiler flags used in this work---\AgdaFlag{safe} and \AgdaFlag{without-K}---restrict the formal environment further. No postulates can be introduced, and no appeal to the uniqueness of identity proofs is permitted. These flags do not create the surviving structure; they ensure that the execution cannot smuggle in extra freedom while the eliminative argument is carried out.

\section{From Cut To Distinction}
\label{sec:formal-threshold:cut-to-distinction}

At the threshold, the pre-formal cut receives a formal representative. The record \texttt{Distinction} is not the Void itself and not the metaphysical origin of difference. It is the MLTT presentation of the minimal data needed for the later eliminator:

\begin{enumerate}
\item a carrier \texttt{S : Set}, so there is a domain in which positions can be addressed;
\item two boundary points \texttt{ℓ} and \texttt{r}, so the cut has sides;
\item a separation witness \texttt{ℓ≠r}, so the sides do not collapse;
\item a cover, so every element of the carrier is classified by one of the two sides.
\end{enumerate}

The cover is crucial. MLTT does not allow the inference from ``only two points have been named'' to ``there are no other points.'' Such an inference would confuse syntax with ontology. If the formal carrier is to be exactly binary for the purposes of elimination, the coverage has to be part of the data. This is why the record is precise rather than romantic: it states exactly what the formal machine needs, and nothing it cannot justify.

\section{Reader Contract}
\label{sec:formal-threshold:reader-contract}

After this point the text changes status. The prose may still motivate, orient, and interpret, but the mathematical claims are tied to the Agda development that follows. A construction must be an inhabitant. An equality must reduce or be proved. A contradiction must have no branch. A classification must cover all cases. A uniqueness claim must state the relevant equivalence and close it.

The first code block therefore does not begin the ontology. It begins the execution. The threshold has already forced the demand for a cut at the level of boundary argument; the formal file now receives that demand as explicit data and lets the checker eliminate whatever cannot survive it. This is the spine of the whole project: claim, data, execution, closure, and interpretation must remain connected without being confused.

\part{Foundation}

The formal development begins by fixing the minimal logical infrastructure on which the later combinatorial and arithmetic arguments depend. Equality, pairing, negation, and the natural numbers are often treated as background. Here they are introduced explicitly so that later uniqueness claims rest on a fully visible formal basis.

This choice is methodological rather than polemical. Before any graph-theoretic or spectral argument can be evaluated, the ambient logic has to be specified carefully enough that no hidden axiom or informal convention can influence the outcome.

\chapter{Minimal Logical Infrastructure}
\label{ch:foundation-necessity}

The first task is to specify the formal environment itself. In Agda, constructive work depends not only on the definitions one writes but also on the background principles permitted by the language.

The flag \AgdaFlag{safe} excludes postulates and ensures that no external axiom is introduced silently. The flag \AgdaFlag{without-K} avoids the additional identification of all equality proofs and keeps the treatment of identity compatible with standard homotopy-theoretic practice. Universe levels provide the usual stratification that prevents impredicative self-reference.

None of this is peculiar to the present text. These are standard structural restrictions, recorded here because the later arguments use them repeatedly and because the opening code block is easiest to read once its ambient assumptions have been stated explicitly.

\AgdaPragma{--without-K}\AgdaSpace{}%

\end{code}

\section{Propositional Equality}
\label{sec:foundation:propositional-equality}

A formal development needs an internal notion of equality before it can state substitution, transport, or congruence. In the Martin-Löf type theory used here for the formal execution, this role is played by the identity type.

The definition used here is the standard one: an inductive family generated by reflexivity. From that single constructor one obtains symmetry, transitivity, congruence, and substitution by straightforward pattern matching on \texttt{refl}. No additional extensional principle is introduced in this development.

\section{Universe Lifting}
\label{sec:foundation:universe-lifting}

Universe stratification prevents self-reference, but it also creates a practical issue: data living at one level cannot simply be reused at the next. The standard remedy is \texttt{Lift}, which places a value in a higher universe without changing its content.

The accompanying lemmas record the two properties that matter later. First, the embedding is faithful: equality between lifted values reflects equality between the originals. Second, \texttt{Lift} satisfies the expected universal property, so any wrapper with exact round-trip behaviour is canonically isomorphic to it under that requirement.

\section{Products and Dependent Pairs}
\label{sec:foundation:products-dependent-pairs}

So far, every structure holds a single piece of information. But the moment a statement like ``there exists an element with a certain property'' must be expressed, two things must be held at once: the element and the proof of its property. Without a way to bundle these together, existential statements are inexpressible inside this constructive setting. The system can talk about individual objects but cannot witness claims about them.

The product type (\texttt{A × B}) is the simplest response: it holds two independent values side by side. But the more consequential structure is the dependent pair (\texttt{Σ A B}), where the type of the second component depends on the value of the first. This is what makes it possible to say ``there exists an $a$ in $A$ such that $B(a)$ holds''—the $a$ and its proof travel together as a single witness. Without dependent pairs, the development would have universal statements but no internal form of existential witness.

The formal apparatus is correspondingly lean. The record \texttt{\_×\_}
handles the non-dependent case of two pieces of data carried together,
while \texttt{Σ} expresses the genuinely existential case in which the
second component depends on the first. From this point on, existential
claims in the book are not verbal gestures but inhabitants of
\texttt{Σ}-types, with ordinary products as the constant special case.

\section{Absurdity and Negation}
\label{sec:foundation:absurdity-negation}

If the filter described in the introduction is to have any teeth, it must be possible to express that something \textit{cannot} exist. A system that can only affirm—never deny—has no elimination power. Under such a regime, incompatible candidates would remain indistinguishable from admissible ones.

The empty type (\texttt{⊥}) is the formal expression of impossibility: a type with no constructors, and therefore no inhabitants. If one were to hold a value of type \texttt{⊥}, a contradiction would already have been reached, and from that contradiction anything follows. This is \texttt{⊥-elim}, the principle of \textit{ex falso quodlibet}: from the impossible, derive whatever you wish.

Negation falls out immediately. To say ``$A$ is false'' is to say ``$A$ leads to a contradiction''—formally, $\neg A$ is the function type $A \to \bot$. No separate negation primitive is added. Double negation and inequality are then derived forms, not new axioms.

The code reflects exactly this economy. The type \texttt{⊥} has no
constructors, \texttt{⊥-elim} is its eliminator, and negation is defined
directly as the function type $A \to \bot$. Refutation is therefore not
an external meta-principle but part of the same internal calculus as
construction.

\section{Disjoint Union}
\label{sec:foundation:disjoint-union}

Pairs express ``both A and B.'' But logic also requires ``either A or B''—and it requires knowing \textit{which one}. An untagged alternative—where the two cases are merged without a label—destroys the ability to distinguish them. Case analysis becomes impossible.

The disjoint union (\texttt{A ⊎ B}) solves this by tagging each side: \texttt{inj₁} marks a witness from the left, \texttt{inj₂} from the right. Pattern matching can then determine which case holds. The $\mathit{Set}_\omega$ variant (\texttt{\_⊎ω\_}) extends this to the top universe level, for the same reason equality was extended to all levels: the later arguments quantify at that height and need the same tagged alternatives there.

Again the formal mechanism is minimal. The datatype \texttt{\_⊎\_}
stores the two tagged alternatives, and \texttt{\_⊎ω\_} repeats the
same construction at the top universe. Every later binary split in the
book, including the coverage data of \texttt{Distinction}, is simply an
instance of pattern matching on this tagged sum.

\section{Stabilized Contact}
\label{sec:foundation:stabilized-contact}

Once products, dependent pairs, equality, and tagged alternatives are
available, contact can be stated without adding a new primitive.  Given
two evaluations into a common carrier, contact is the dependent witness
that one origin from the first source and one origin from the second
source share an image.  It is not a metaphysical bond between completed
objects; it is synchronized retrievability carried as data.

Self-contact is the decisive test.  An evaluation is stable only if its
self-contact does not hide a collapse: whenever two origins become equal
after evaluation, the origins were already equal.  In that case the
self-contact carries no surplus over the origin.  The diagonal is not
postulated from outside; it is recovered as the residue of non-collapse.

Agreement zones and stable relations are the first two shapes obtained
from this discipline.  An agreement zone records the positions at which
two evaluations cease to differ.  A stable relation is a pair of
evaluations whose combined imprint does not identify distinct origins.
These constructions occur after the formal threshold.  They do not prove
that the pre-formal boundary is itself a type; they show what becomes
available once a disciplined carrier, equality, and dependent witnesses
are already in force.

\section{Ontological Primitives}
\label{sec:foundation:ontological-primitives}

Before distinction itself is defined, three auxiliary predicates fix the local vocabulary. A contractible type has a center to which every inhabitant is equal, and therefore carries no internal separation. A type with a distinct pair contains two provably different elements. Non-triviality is simply the negation of contractibility.

These notions provide the vocabulary for the next stage of the argument. They make precise what it means for a carrier to admit a genuine boundary and prepare the non-contractibility results used shortly afterward.

\section{The Distinction Record}
\label{sec:foundation:distinction-record}

Formally, a distinction consists of a carrier, two designated elements of that carrier, a proof that these elements are different, and a cover asserting that every element of the carrier coincides with one of them. This is precisely the data required for the two-case eliminator developed in the next chapter; anything less would leave either separation or coverage unavailable.

The cover is not an ornamental extra. Without it one would have two marked points but no uniform way to classify arbitrary elements of the carrier, and the later elimination arguments would lose their basic case split. The counterexample below makes that dependence explicit rather than rhetorical.

\subsection{Necessity of Coverage}
\label{sec:foundation:cover-necessary}

The separation proof and the cover serve different purposes. It is natural to ask whether the cover might be recovered from the two designated boundary points alone. The answer is negative under the displayed data. On a carrier with more than two distinguishable elements, an eliminator based only on the boundary witnesses fails, because an off-boundary element need not satisfy a predicate determined at those two points.

The four-element vertex type $K_4\mathrm{Vertex}$, introduced later in Chapter~\ref{ch:k4-representation-theory}, provides a concrete witness to this failure. Lemma~\ref{lem:cover-necessary} records the argument formally. The cover is therefore part of the definition for operational reasons: it is what makes global two-case elimination possible.

\subsection*{Minimal presentation in MLTT}
\label{sec:foundation:minimality-declaration}

The five fields of \texttt{Distinction} --- the carrier $S$, the two boundary points $\ell$ and $r$, the separation proof $\ell \neq r$, and the cover --- are stated here as the minimal presentation sufficient for the elimination framework developed in this text. Each field is operationally indispensable: the carrier alone has no second point to compare to, the boundary points without separation collapse to a singleton, and the cover cannot be derived from the separated pair --- Lemma~\ref{lem:cover-necessary} refutes any such derivation by exhibiting $K_4\mathrm{Vertex}$ as a four-element counterexample. There is no way to remove a field and recover the elimination chain that follows.

What this presentation does \emph{not} claim is the stronger reading sometimes attached to ``minimality": that naming only $\ell$ and $r$ as inhabitants of $S$ would, by itself, force $S$ to contain no third element. Standard Martin-L\"of type theory does not validate that step; it admits types with elements not produced by any named constructor and provides no internal mechanism that turns ``not introduced" into ``does not exist". The cover field is therefore not a workaround. It is the explicit specification of two-class coverage that the type theory cannot supply for free; it is the exact data that must be provided explicitly, since it cannot be reconstructed within the theory.

\chapter{Non-Vacuity}
\label{ch:non-vacuity}

The record \texttt{Distinction} has now been defined, but a definition alone does not produce an inhabitant. If \texttt{Distinction} were empty, then every universal statement about distinctions would hold vacuously, and the subsequent development would lose substantive force. The purpose of this chapter is to block that collapse in the weakest form needed at the outset.

Under \AgdaFlag{safe}, no inhabitant of \texttt{Distinction} is simply postulated. The statement used here is the double-negation form $\neg\neg\,\mathit{Distinction}$. It does not yet supply a witness, but it excludes stable denial and is exactly the weaker non-vacuity guard needed before the later constructive witness appears.

Stronger results appear later. Chapter~\ref{ch:two-normal-form} constructs \texttt{Two-distinction} without premises, and Chapter~\ref{ch:scale-closure} provides an independent route through measurement. By contrast, the stronger claim that every inhabited type already contains a distinction is false; the unit type $\top$ is the standard counterexample. The present chapter therefore uses the weaker formulation because it is both correct and sufficient for what follows.

\subsection{Law 0.4: Distinction Carrier Is Non-Contractible}
\label{law:nonvacuity:non-contractible}

\subsection{Law 0.7: Reconstruction Is Exact}
\label{law:nonvacuity:reconstruction-exact}

This reconstruction is exact in the strongest available sense. If one extracts the fields of a distinction and feeds them back into the constructor, the result is definitionally equal to the original term, so the proof is simply \texttt{refl}.

\begin{code}%
\>[0]\AgdaComment{--\ §\ Law\ 0.7:\ Reconstruction\ is\ exact\ by\ definitional\ equality.}\<%
\\
\>[0]\AgdaFunction{law0-7-reconstruction-exact}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{:}\<%
\\
\>[0][@{}l@{\AgdaIndent{0}}]%
\>[2]\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaRecord{Distinction}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{→}\<%
\\
%
\>[2]\AgdaFunction{fromDistinctCovered}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaField{ℓ}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaField{r}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaField{ℓ≠r}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaField{cover}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaOperator{\AgdaDatatype{≡}}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\<%
\\
\>[0]\AgdaFunction{law0-7-reconstruction-exact}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{=}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaInductiveConstructor{refl}\<%
\end{code}

The record may therefore be unpacked and reassembled without loss. Later arguments use this observation when moving between the record itself and its component data.

\chapter{Elimination and Classification}
\label{ch:elimination-classification}

Once a distinction is fixed, the associated endomorphism space is severely constrained. Because the cover identifies every element of the carrier with either $\ell$ or $r$, an endomorphism is determined entirely by its values on those two points. The boundary-output table therefore has at most four entries.

This chapter makes that observation precise and uses it to derive the four-function configuration that later reappears as $K_4$.

\section{Two-Class Coverage}
\label{sec:classification:two-class-coverage}

\subsection{Law 1.1: Carrier Coverage Is Two-Class}
\label{law:classification:two-class-coverage}

The first classification lemma is just the cover field restated for later use. Its importance is practical rather than subtle: every subsequent case distinction on the carrier depends on the fact that the cover reduces all elements to these two classes.

\begin{code}%
\>[0]\AgdaComment{--\ §\ Law\ 1.1:\ Carrier\ coverage\ is\ two-class.}\<%
\\
\>[0]\AgdaFunction{law1-1-cover}\AgdaSpace{}%

\AgdaField{S}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{d}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{→}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaBound{x}\AgdaSpace{}%

\\

\end{code}

Two-class coverage is the first structural restriction on the carrier. Figure~\ref{fig:first-distinction} records this dichotomy as a two-node distinction diagram.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex, node distance=3.2cm]
  \node[circle, draw=fdBlue, thick, minimum size=10mm, fill=fdLight] (l) {$\ell$};
  \node[circle, draw=fdRed, thick, minimum size=10mm, fill=fdLight, right of=l] (r) {$r$};
  \draw[->, thick] (l) -- node[above] {distinction} (r);
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Binary distinction data: two boundary witnesses forced by two-class coverage.}
\label{fig:first-distinction}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Law 1.2: Elimination Is Forced By Coverage}
\label{law:classification:elimination-from-coverage}

Coverage yields a canonical eliminator for predicates on the carrier. If a property $P$ is known at the two boundary points $\ell$ and $r$, then it is known everywhere, because the cover reduces every input to one of those two cases. The uniqueness lemma below records the corresponding rigidity: any eliminator satisfying the same boundary equations agrees with the canonical one everywhere.

Formally, the point is straightforward. Any eliminator that agrees with
\texttt{Distinction-elim} on the two boundary witnesses must inspect
$\mathrm{cover}\,d\,x$, and this case split leaves only the same two
branches. The boundary equations then force the values to coincide, so
the alleged alternative reduces to pointwise equality with the canonical
eliminator. The dependent eliminator inherits the same rigidity through
transport.

\section{Duality}
\label{sec:classification:duality}

Once the carrier has been reduced to the two boundary classes, there is a canonical nontrivial self-map obtained by exchanging them. This map, called \emph{duality}, sends $\ell$ to $r$ and $r$ to $\ell$. Later results close the classification absolutely: up to pointwise equality, it is the only non-identity automorphism of a distinction.

Its basic property is involutivity. Because every element of the carrier is identified by the cover with one of the two boundary points, applying the swap twice returns the original element after a short case analysis.

\section{Pointwise Equality}
\label{sec:classification:pointwise-equality}

To compare endomorphisms, the natural relation is pointwise equality. Two functions are identified when they agree at every argument. On a distinction this relation is especially effective, because the cover reduces every input to one of the two boundary cases.

The universal property below states this explicitly. Any relation on endomorphisms that already determines agreement on the two boundary points refines to pointwise equality on the whole carrier under the cover.

\section{Four-Case Endomorphism Classification}
\label{sec:classification:four-case-endomorphism-classification}

An endomorphism $f : S \to S$ is determined by the pair of values $f(\ell)$ and $f(r)$. Since each of these values must be either $\ell$ or $r$, exactly four candidate combinations arise:

\begin{itemize}
\item $f(\ell) = \ell$ and $f(r) = \ell$: the constant-left map.
\item $f(\ell) = r$ and $f(r) = r$: the constant-right map.
\item $f(\ell) = \ell$ and $f(r) = r$: the identity.
\item $f(\ell) = r$ and $f(r) = \ell$: the dual.
\end{itemize}

The soundness proof below turns these four candidates into an exhaustive classification of the endomorphism space. The datatype \texttt{EndoCase} is introduced simply to name them once and for all.

\begin{code}%
\>[0]\AgdaComment{--\ §\ The\ four-case\ classification\ of\ endomorphisms.}\<%
\\
\>[0]\AgdaKeyword{data}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaDatatype{EndoCase}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaPrimitive{Set}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaKeyword{where}\<%
\\
\>[0][@{}l@{\AgdaIndent{0}}]%
\>[2]\AgdaInductiveConstructor{case-constL}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaDatatype{EndoCase}\<%
\\
%
\>[2]\AgdaInductiveConstructor{case-constR}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaDatatype{EndoCase}\<%
\\
%
\>[2]\AgdaInductiveConstructor{case-id}%
\>[14]\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaDatatype{EndoCase}\<%
\\
%
\>[2]\AgdaInductiveConstructor{case-dual}%
\>[14]\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaDatatype{EndoCase}\<%
\end{code}

Figure~\ref{fig:k3-failure} illustrates the basic obstruction behind the later appearance of $K_4$: a three-vertex closure cannot accommodate four distinct endomorphism cases without omission.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex, every node/.style={circle, draw=fdBlue, thick, minimum size=9mm, fill=fdLight}]
  \node (a) at (90:1.8) {$c_L$};
  \node (b) at (210:1.8) {$c_R$};
  \node (c) at (330:1.8) {$id$};
  \node[draw=fdRed, text=fdRed, right=2.8cm of c] (d) {$dual$};
  \draw[thick] (a) -- (b) -- (c) -- cycle;
  \draw[dashed, thick, fdRed, ->] (d) -- ($(b)!0.5!(c)$);
  \node[rectangle, rounded corners=1mm, draw=fdRed, text=fdRed, fill=white, below=0.2cm of d] {unstable on $K_3$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{The failure of $K_3$: the four mathematically distinct endomorphism cases cannot close over three vertices. One function is structurally forced into non-closure.}
\label{fig:k3-failure}
\end{figure}

\section{The \texorpdfstring{$K_4$}{K4} Classification Module}
\label{sec:classification:k4-module}

The four cases are only names until they are related back to actual endomorphisms of the carrier. The \texttt{K₄} module packages the corresponding constructions: the endomorphisms themselves, pointwise equality, the four representatives, and the maps that interpret and classify them. The parameter $d$ keeps the whole discussion relative to a fixed distinction.

\paragraph{Step 6: Classification uniqueness.}
Soundness and injectivity together show that the label assigned by
\texttt{classify} is unique. Here the absolute statement is local and
proved: once a case label interprets to the same endomorphism, it must
be the classifier's label.

\begin{code}%
%
\>[2]\AgdaComment{--\ §\ Classification\ is\ unique:\ the\ label\ is\ forced\ by\ soundness\ +\ injectivity.}\<%

\AgdaFunction{Endo}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{→}\AgdaSpace{}%

\AgdaSymbol{:}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaDatatype{EndoCase}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%

\AgdaBound{f}\AgdaSpace{}%

\paragraph{Step 7: The classifier is a left-inverse of interpretation.}
Applying the uniqueness statement to $f := \mathit{interpret}\,c$
shows that classification is a left inverse to interpretation.

\begin{code}%

\AgdaSymbol{→}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaFunction{classify}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{(}\AgdaFunction{interpret}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{c}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaOperator{\AgdaDatatype{≡}}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{c}\<%
\\
%
\>[2]\AgdaFunction{classify-interpret}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{c}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaSymbol{=}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaFunction{sym}\AgdaSpace{}%

\AgdaBound{c}\AgdaSymbol{)}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaBound{c}\AgdaSpace{}%
\AgdaFunction{≗-refl}\AgdaSymbol{)}\<%
\end{code}

\chapter{Two Normal Form}
\label{ch:two-normal-form}

The endomorphism space has now been classified completely, but the carrier $S$ of a distinction is still abstract. Coverage reduces it to two boundary classes; what is not yet fixed is the explicit normal form of that carrier. This chapter supplies that normal form and proves that every distinction reaches it.

The cover yields maps in both directions between an arbitrary distinction carrier and the type \texttt{Two}. These maps are inverse up to the expected equalities, so under the conditions already fixed every distinction carrier is forced into isomorphism with a two-element type. At that point the remaining variation is not hidden structure; it is orientation, whether $\ell$ corresponds to \texttt{L} or to \texttt{R}.

\section{The Two Type}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:two-type}

The datatype \texttt{Two} is the explicit two-element object used to display that normal form. Its two constructors are distinct, and its cover is immediate by pattern matching. The later isomorphism theorem, not naming convention, makes it the normal form for arbitrary distinction carriers.

This supplies the constructive witness whose existence was deferred in Chapter~\ref{ch:non-vacuity}. The object \texttt{Two-distinction} inhabits \texttt{Distinction} without further hypotheses, and it will be used throughout the remainder of the text whenever a concrete distinction is required.

\section{Marked Subcarriers}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:marked-subcarriers}

Once \texttt{Two} has appeared, a carrier can be read by the two sides
of the normal form.  Such a reading is only a marking, not a hidden
principle that classifies every predicate automatically.  A predicate
becomes a mark only when a constructive decision procedure accompanies
it; without that decision, no side can be assigned without adding
information not present in the predicate itself.

The marked subcarriers are therefore fibers of a displayed map into
\texttt{Two}.  The left fiber contains exactly the points marked
\texttt{L}; the right fiber contains exactly the points marked
\texttt{R}.  The cover of \texttt{Two} then gives a two-way reading for
each marked point, while the predicate construction records the honest
direction: decidability produces a marker, not arbitrary truth.

\section{Classifier Objects}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:classifier-objects}

The binary marker is not the last possible form of classification.  A
richer formal environment may carry a truth carrier with more structure
than \texttt{Two}.  What cannot change is the skeleton of classification:
there must be a carrier of marks, an acknowledged truth point, a map from
the object being read into that carrier, and a selected fiber over the
truth point.

This does not import a categorical axiom into the development.  The code
below records the exact data that any such classifier must display before
it can classify anything at all.  The binary classifier is then recovered
as the first case: \texttt{Two} with \texttt{L} as the truth point.  Thus
the richer truth object is not identified with \texttt{Two}; it is a later
generalization of the same marking discipline.

\section{Distinction Cover as Binary Fiber}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:distinction-cover-binary-fiber}

The cover field of a distinction now has a direct reading in the marking
language.  It is not a classifier for arbitrary predicates on the
carrier.  It is the displayed binary reading already present in the
record: each point of the carrier is read as belonging to the left
boundary class or to the right boundary class.

Under this marker the two fibers recover exactly the two boundary
classes.  The left fiber is the class of points equal to $\ell$; the
right fiber is the class of points equal to $r$.  Thus the cover does
not hover as an external condition over the carrier.  Once \texttt{Two}
is available, it is the first fiber presentation of the distinction
itself.

\section{Stable Classified Contact}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:stable-classified-contact}

The point of contact with richer mathematical languages is now visible.
A later theory may speak of relations, characteristic maps, truth values,
or classified subobjects.  Those names are harmless when their data are
displayed.  What matters is that relation, stability, and classification
arrive together: a joint imprint must not collapse origins, and the
selected part of the origin carrier must be the truth fiber of a
displayed marker.

This is an interface of union, not rivalry.  It does not deny later
languages their own constructions.  It asks them to expose the contact
data by which those constructions become readable: two evaluations, a
non-collapsing joint imprint, a classifier object, and a characteristic
map into that classifier.  Once those are present, the selected
subcarrier is no longer a free predicate hovering over the system; it is
the fiber forced by the truth anchor.

The interface is now closed in the modest sense appropriate here.  A
stable classified contact is not recovered from a selected fiber alone:
the fiber remembers classification, not the two evaluations whose joint
imprint was stable.  But once those evaluations, their stability witness,
and the marker are displayed, no further datum is needed to assemble the
interface.  The binary classifier is also not a metaphor for the general
case; it is the definitional first case of the same pattern.  Finally,
stability may be transported only through maps that do not collapse
information.  This last condition is essential: arbitrary
postcomposition can identify values and destroy stability.

\section{Stable Reading Interface}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:stable-reading-interface}

The previous constructions can now be collected without naming any
later language.  The interface records only the roles that have already
appeared: a carrier being read, two displayed readings of it, a
non-collapsing joint imprint, and a marker into a classifier object.
It is the stable reading surface on which richer structures can later
display their data.

The point of the record is architectural.  It makes the translation
surface explicit while keeping the level fixed.  From a stable reading
one obtains a stable classified contact, a classified truth fiber, and
contact with the truth point.  Conversely, the first binary instance is
already present in a distinction: the cover determines a marker, and the
separation of the two boundary classes makes that marker non-collapsing.

\section{From Stable Reading to Morphism}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:stable-reading-morphism}

A stable reading presents one object of the classifier interface.  The
categorical layer begins by comparing such presentations through maps
that preserve the displayed readings, the classifier marker, and the
non-collapsing origin data.

A structure-preserving map carries origins, left readings, and right
readings forward; it makes the two reading squares commute; it preserves
the classifier marker; and its origin map is non-collapsing.  The last
condition prevents transport from identifying origins that were separated
before transport.  Such an identification would not preserve the reading;
it would collapse the presentation being read.

These maps supply the first category data for stable readings: objects,
homs, identities, composition, and the corresponding laws.  The laws are
stated up to visible equality of the three displayed maps rather than
equality of all proof fields.  This keeps the construction inside the
same intensional discipline used from the beginning and avoids assuming
function extensionality.

\section{Reindexing and Pullback Shape}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:reindexing-pullback-shape}

With structure maps in place, reindexing becomes the first categorical
test.  A marker visible at the target of a structure map has a controlled
preimage at the source.  In ordinary categorical language this is the
beginning of pullback behaviour: the target marker is pulled back along
the origin map, compared with the source marker, and carried together
with its truth fiber and contact with the truth point.

The statement is local.  It records the pullback-shaped square carried by
a single stable reading morphism, not a global supply of pullbacks in the
ambient category.  The comparison part is isolated below through
mono-like subcarrier data and cone comparison maps.  Here the point is
that classified visibility at the target has a stable preimage at the
source, obtained by composing with the structure map already displayed.

\section{Mono-Like Subcarrier Data}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:mono-like-subcarrier-data}

The previous section isolated the square-shaped behaviour of a pulled
fiber.  The next ingredient is the selected carrier itself.  A classified
subcarrier is already equivalent to a truth fiber, but its inclusion into
the ambient carrier must be displayed before any later categorical
language can speak honestly about monic behaviour.

There is a small intensional point here.  The selected carrier may carry
proof data, and equality of proof data is not assumed.  The record below
is therefore not a categorical monomorphism.  It records the visible
inclusion into the ambient carrier and equips it with a visible equality:
two selected points agree when their displayed ambient points agree.  This
is the amount of monic behaviour used by the constructions below.

\section{Visible Pullback Comparison}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:visible-pullback-comparison}

The pullback shape can now be tested against arbitrary comparison data.
Suppose a carrier maps to the source reading and also displays a point of
the target truth fiber.  If those two displays agree after applying the
structure map, then it already determines a point of the canonical
pulled-back truth fiber.  This is the comparison map that an ordinary
pullback universal property would demand.

The comparison is stated at the visible projection level.  The target
fiber carries proof data, and no proof irrelevance is assumed.  Therefore
the comparison below commutes with the target fiber after projecting to
the displayed target point, and its uniqueness is uniqueness over the
visible source projection.  Every compatible square factors through the
canonical pulled-back fiber, and any other such factorization is visibly
the same at the ambient carrier.

\section{Univalence Boundary}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:univalence-boundary}

Univalence marks the boundary between isomorphism and identity.  In a
univalent setting, equivalent structures can be read as identical along a
path in the universe.  The formal development here does not assume that
principle.  It is checked under \AgdaFlag{safe} and
\AgdaFlag{without-K}; no axiom is postulated, and equality of records is
not enlarged by an external identification principle.

The available direction is identity-to-isomorphism.  An actual identity
of stable readings gives an isomorphism of stable readings: transport
along \texttt{refl} yields identity structure maps in both directions.
The converse direction, from isomorphism back to identity, is the
univalent bridge.  It is displayed below as a record type naming the
additional principle, not as an inhabitant used by the construction.

The orientation data already show why the distinction theorem lands at
isomorphism before identity.  A distinction contains displayed left and
right boundary points.  The two-element carrier can therefore be
presented with those boundaries exchanged.  That swapped presentation is
still a distinction and is isomorphic to \texttt{Two-distinction}; but on
the fixed carrier \texttt{Two}, its displayed left boundary differs from
the canonical displayed left boundary.  A literal record identity would
therefore have to identify presentation data that the theorem itself only
relates by boundary-preserving isomorphism.  Any later identity reading
must quotient or identify presentations beyond the intensional record
equality used here.

\section{Distinction Isomorphism}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:distinction-isomorphism}

To compare distinctions, two related notions are useful. A \texttt{DistinctionIso} is a boundary-preserving isomorphism: it consists of inverse maps between the carriers that also send the distinguished boundary points to their counterparts. A \texttt{DistinctionEquiv} forgets this boundary data and remembers only the underlying equivalence.

Both notions are needed later. The stricter one is appropriate for normal-form statements, while the weaker one is the natural language for orientation and automorphism arguments.

\section{Canonical Two Maps}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:canonical-two-maps}

For any distinction there are structurally determined maps to and from \texttt{Two}. The map \texttt{toTwo} sends an element to \texttt{L} or \texttt{R} according to the cover, while \texttt{fromTwo} sends the two constructors back to the distinguished boundary points.

The auxiliary lemmas \texttt{toTwo-ℓ} and \texttt{toTwo-r} record the behaviour of the forward map on the boundary. The round-trip identities then show that these maps form a boundary-preserving isomorphism.

\section{Presentation Quotient Shape}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:presentation-quotient-shape}

The normal-form theorem supplies the data needed before a quotient can be
taken.  The raw objects are distinctions.  The admissible presentation
relation is boundary-preserving isomorphism, and that relation is
reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.  Every raw distinction also has a
displayed route, not by record identity but by presentation equivalence,
to the canonical representative \texttt{Two-distinction}.

This is not a quotient type.  It is the quotient shape: the object class,
the admissible equivalence relation, the canonical representative, and
the checked normalization map into that representative.  A quotient,
skeleton, or univalent completion can use this data to turn presentation
equivalence into equality of representatives.

\section{Canonical Skeleton Representative}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:canonical-skeleton-representative}

The quotient shape can be sharpened into a skeleton layer without
constructing a quotient type.  The skeleton has one displayed object: the
canonical two-element distinction.  Normalization sends every raw
distinction to that skeleton object, and the soundness proof is exactly
the normal-form isomorphism already established.

This skeleton is not record identity for raw presentations.  It is a
choice of canonical representative together with a checked route from
each raw presentation to that representative through presentation
equivalence.

\section{Stable Reading Skeleton}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:stable-reading-skeleton}

The skeleton also lifts to the stable readings that arise from
distinctions.  This is not a statement about arbitrary stable readings;
it concerns the readings produced by the distinction marker.  A
boundary-preserving isomorphism of distinctions induces an isomorphism of
their displayed stable readings, so the normal-form isomorphism carries
each distinction-induced reading to the canonical reading of
\texttt{Two-distinction}.

\section{Quotient Boundary}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:quotient-boundary}

The skeleton layer identifies a canonical representative, but it still
does not replace presentation equivalence by record identity.  The
additional step would be an identity principle saying that
boundary-preserving presentation equivalence may be read as equality of
raw distinction records.  The present construction names that principle
without assuming it.

\section{Subobject Classifier Test}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:subobject-classifier-test}

The classifier interface already classifies its own truth fibers.  Every
marker determines a selected carrier, that selected carrier has a visible
inclusion into the ambient carrier, and the characteristic map is the
marker with which the fiber was formed.  This is the classifier-shaped
part of the construction.

The full subobject-classifier strength is stronger.  It would require a
universal comparison saying that every admissible subobject is classified
uniquely by such a characteristic map, in the chosen equality of
subobjects.  The record below separates the truth-fiber data from that
stronger universal extension.

\section{Topos Boundary Map}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:topos-boundary-map}

The categorical surface contains several checked components: category data
for stable readings, local reindexing, visible pullback comparison,
classifier-shaped truth fibers, and skeleton data for
distinction-induced presentations.  These components are enough to show
where a topos-oriented continuation would attach.  They are not enough to
assert that the stable-reading category is a topos.

The missing strength is also visible: global pullbacks for arbitrary
spans, a universal subobject classifier in the selected equality of
subobjects, exponentials, and an identity or quotient principle turning
presentation equivalence into equality of representatives.

\section{Categorical Closure Overview}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:categorical-closure-overview}

The route through this chapter can be summarized without upgrading
any claim beyond its proof.  The distinction data yield stable readings;
stable readings carry category data; structure maps reindex markers and
truth fibers; mono-like inclusions make selected subcarriers visible;
compatible cones factor through the pulled-back truth fiber at the
visible projection level; distinction presentations normalize to the
canonical skeleton representative; and the quotient and topos boundaries
name the additional principles that would be needed for stronger
identity and topos claims.

\section{Orientation}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:orientation}

An equivalence between a distinction and \texttt{Two} must send the two boundary witnesses to distinct images, because otherwise the inverse map would identify $\ell$ and $r$. Since \texttt{Two} has exactly two elements, the classification closes absolutely here: either the order of the boundary points is preserved or it is swapped.

The following definitions record these two orientations explicitly.

\section{Automorphisms}
\label{sec:two-normal-form:automorphisms}

An automorphism of a distinction is an equivalence from the carrier to itself. Since the carrier has only two boundary classes, the admissible boundary behaviour closes to two possibilities: preserve the boundary points or exchange them. The proofs below make this precise by combining injectivity with the cover.

This completes the automorphism analysis for distinctions. Figure~\ref{fig:k4-orbits}
records the induced symmetry action on the four endomorphism witnesses.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex, every node/.style={circle, draw=fdBlue, thick, minimum size=9mm, fill=fdLight}]
  \node (a) at (90:2.2) {$c_L$};
  \node (b) at (0:2.2) {$c_R$};
  \node (c) at (270:2.2) {$id$};
  \node (d) at (180:2.2) {$dual$};
  \draw[thick] (a) -- (b) -- (c) -- (d) -- (a);
  \draw[dashed, thick] (a) -- (c);
  \draw[dashed, thick] (b) -- (d);
  \draw[->, very thick, fdRed] ($(a)+(0.0,0.35)$) arc[start angle=90,end angle=0,radius=2.2];
  \draw[->, very thick, fdRed] ($(c)+(0.0,-0.35)$) arc[start angle=270,end angle=180,radius=2.2];
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Automorphism action on the four-case witness space: preserve and swap survive as the only orbit structure.}
\label{fig:k4-orbits}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Law 1.9: The Two Isomorphism Is Unique}
\label{law:two-normal-form:isomorphism-unique}

Any boundary-preserving isomorphism from a distinction to \texttt{Two}
agrees with the normal-form map. This is another application of the
eliminator: once the values at $\ell$ and $r$ are fixed, the map is fixed
everywhere. The same reasoning determines the inverse map.

\subsection{Law 1.10: Two Normal Form Has Exactly Two Orientations}
\label{law:two-normal-form:two-orientations}

orientations just described. This is an absolute classification because
the proof eliminates the two equal-image cases by contradiction.

\subsection{Law 1.11: Automorphisms Are Exactly id Or dual}
\label{law:two-normal-form:automorphisms-id-or-dual}

Automorphisms are therefore exhausted by the identity and the dual map.
The word ``exactly'' is justified by \texttt{Aut-sound}: preservation and
exchange are the only boundary behaviours compatible with injectivity and
coverage.

\subsection{Law 1.12: Two-Orientation Classification Is Sound And Unique}
\label{law:two-normal-form:orientation-classification}

The next step packages the two orientations into an explicit classifier.
Each equivalence to \texttt{Two} receives one of two labels,
\texttt{case-preserve} or \texttt{case-swap}, together with a proof that
the chosen label reproduces the map. Uniqueness is immediate because the
two interpretations already disagree at the left boundary point; to let a
single equivalence realize both would force $L \equiv R$.

\subsection{Law 1.13: Automorphism Classification Is Sound And Unique}
\label{law:two-normal-form:automorphism-classification}

This final classification statement records the same two properties as
before: under the two-class constraint every automorphism falls into one
of the two surviving forms, and that form is uniquely determined.

\section{K\texorpdfstring{$_4$}{4} Witness Interface}
\label{sec:classification:k4-witness-interface}

The classification results for endomorphisms are now packaged once more
in witness form. For a given endomorphism, the witness consists of a case
label together with a proof that the interpreted case agrees pointwise
with the original map. This adds no new assumption; it exposes the earlier
module-level statements as a global interface.

\section{Two-Class Coverage Without Definitional Equality}
\label{sec:classification:coverage-without-definitional-equality}

Up to this point the development has used propositional equality throughout. For later applications the elimination argument must be separated from that particular equality relation and stated instead for an arbitrary equivalence relation.

The record \texttt{DistinctionClass} provides this generalization in explicit form. It consists of a carrier equipped with a reflexive, symmetric, and transitive relation, together with two distinguished elements that remain separate under that relation and a corresponding two-class cover. The eliminator from the earlier sections then extends to this broader setting without changing its structural role.

\section{Presentation Uniqueness}
\label{sec:presentation:elimination}

The canonical classifier is not the only possible way to index the four endomorphism cases. One may choose a different datatype $X$ together with interpretation and classification maps. The next theorem shows that any such presentation is equivalent to the chosen one, provided it is sound and its interpretation map is injective up to pointwise equality.

In other words, once soundness and injectivity are fixed, the classification is unique up to reindexing. The proof constructs explicit maps between $X$ and \texttt{EndoCase} and then verifies the two round-trip laws.

\subsection{Law 1.19--1.20: Orientation and Automorphism Presentation Uniqueness}
\label{laws:presentation:orientation-automorphism-elimination}

The same argument applies to the orientation and automorphism classifications. Once the classifier/interpreter pair is fixed, any alternative presentation satisfying the same soundness and injectivity requirements is isomorphic to that presentation. The freedom left by relabelling is therefore harmless: it changes names, not structure.

The following helper definitions prepare these two analogues of the endomorphism presentation theorem.

\paragraph{Presentation records.}
A presentation of either classification, orientation or automorphism is a set-valued interface carrying interpretation, classification, soundness, and injectivity. The corresponding records package exactly the data required to compare an arbitrary labeling with the fixed classifier/interpreter pair.
